semantic-models-dax.label: Semantic Models & DAX
semantic-models-dax.description: Original practice questions authored for the Hansa corpus integration from the open MicrosoftLearning course labs (mslearn-fabric, PL-300) and Microsoft Learn documentation. Covers storage modes and Direct Lake, relationships and star-schema design, DAX evaluation context and time intelligence, calculation groups and field parameters, incremental refresh, model security and the XMLA endpoint. No video anchors: every question is documentation-grounded, not video-derived.

questions.title: Two billion rows, no copies
questions.prompt: Harborline Retail's lakehouse holds a Delta fact table with about two billion point-of-sale rows. Planners need a semantic model with sub-second slicing over existing aggregations, the data already lives in OneLake as Delta, and the analytics lead refuses any second copy of the fact data. Which storage mode fits this brief?

options.text: Import mode, refreshed nightly
options.why: Import copies the data into the model, which the lead explicitly refuses, and a nightly refresh misses same-day detail.

options.text: DirectQuery to the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint
options.why: DirectQuery keeps one copy but pushes every visual query to SQL against the endpoint, which rarely meets sub-second slicing targets on a two-billion-row fact.

options.text: Direct Lake over the lakehouse Delta tables
options.why: Correct. Direct Lake reads the OneLake Delta files directly with model-speed in-memory queries and no second copy of the data.

options.text: DirectQuery to the source operational database
options.why: That bypasses Fabric entirely, loads the operational system with analytical queries, and still carries DirectQuery latency.

questions.explanation: Direct Lake exists for exactly this brief: the Delta tables stay the single copy in OneLake, and the model queries them at in-memory speed without an import refresh cycle.

caseStudy.title: Harborline Retail semantic model redesign
caseStudy.text: Harborline Retail runs a Fabric lakehouse (harborline_lake) with Delta tables for roughly two billion point-of-sale rows (fact_sales), product, store, and customer dimensions, and a small daily stock-snapshot fact (fact_stock). The team publishes a Direct Lake semantic model, harborline_sales, on the lakehouse for about 300 store planners. Planners belong to region assignments stored in a planner-region mapping table, and one planner may cover two regions. Finance keeps a separate nightly Import model for regulated reporting. The analytics engineering team ships both models through deployment pipelines and tracks query speed, model size and access reviews monthly. Current friction: a handful of visuals run noticeably slower than the rest, month-start loads overlap with planner working hours, and product hierarchy changes do not appear until someone updates the model.

questions.title: What Direct Lake actually reads
questions.prompt: A reviewer claims the harborline_sales Direct Lake model must be refreshed every morning so its in-memory copy picks up the Delta writes that landed overnight. What is the accurate statement about Direct Lake data availability?

options.text: Correct — a scheduled refresh copies Delta data into the model each night.
options.why: That describes Import mode. Direct Lake does not stage a copied dataset that needs a nightly load.

options.text: Incorrect — Direct Lake reads the OneLake Delta files directly, so new committed Delta versions are queryable without a data refresh.
options.why: Correct. The model reads the same parquet/delta files in OneLake; committed data changes are picked up without an import-style refresh.

options.text: Incorrect — Direct Lake polls the operational database continuously.
options.why: Direct Lake never touches the operational system; it is bound to OneLake artifacts.

options.text: Incorrect — planners must run an XMLA process full on the model after every load.
options.why: A process operation is not required for data changes; schema-affecting changes are the case where the model needs an update.

questions.explanation: Direct Lake's defining property is direct binding to OneLake Delta storage: data changes committed to the Delta tables are visible to the model without an import-style data refresh, while structural changes to the source need a model update.

questions.title: Snowflake or not
questions.prompt: A modeler proposes normalizing the product dimension into separate product-category and product-brand tables, each joined through the product dimension, to keep tables tidy in the semantic model. From a semantic-model design standpoint, what is the strongest argument against this in the model layer?

options.text: Snowflaking saves model memory, which is why semantic models encourage it.
options.why: It does not save meaningful memory in a VertiPaq model and the design cost is real; guidance favors a single denormalized dimension.

options.text: Snowflaked chains complicate filter propagation and make the model harder to browse and maintain.
options.why: Correct. Star-schema guidance keeps one wide, denormalized dimension so filtering stays simple, browsing stays flat, and DAX does not depend on chained relationships.

options.text: Chained one-to-many relationships are not supported in Fabric semantic models.
options.why: They are supported; the objection is design and usability, not capability.

options.text: Category and brand attributes must instead be pushed into the fact table as columns.
options.why: Widening the fact table with repeating descriptive attributes is the anti-pattern, not the fix.

questions.explanation: The star-schema guidance is explicit: keep dimensions denormalized and flat for intuitive browsing and reliable filter propagation; leave normalization to source systems where it belongs.

questions.title: Grain of the stock snapshot
questions.prompt: fact_stock records one row per store, per product, per day at end of day. A developer joins it to fact_sales directly and reports double-counted stock valuation. What is the soundest modeling diagnosis?

options.text: fact_stock needs a surrogate key on every column to block the join.
options.why: Surrogate keys do not fix a grain mismatch; the join itself is the design error.

options.text: The two facts have different grains and must not be joined to each other; each should relate to shared dimensions instead.
options.why: Correct. Facts at different grains are separate fact tables related through conformed dimensions, never directly to each other.

options.text: fact_stock should be filtered to month-end rows before joining so both tables agree.
options.why: Filtering hides the mismatch without removing it; the direct fact-to-fact join is still wrong.

options.text: The stock measure should be divided by the number of sales rows to rebalance it.
options.why: Arithmetic averaging over a join invents a number that corresponds to nothing.

questions.explanation: Grain is the first decision of fact design. Two facts at different grains answer different questions and must each relate to the conformed dimensions, not to one another.

questions.title: Planners and regions
questions.prompt: One planner covers several regions and each region has several planners. A direct planner-to-region relationship is impossible in a one-to-many model. What is the standard star-schema remedy?

options.text: Concatenate planner and region into one key column on both tables.
options.why: A concatenated key still forces one row per pair and cannot represent the group structure cleanly; it also breaks planner-level filtering.

options.text: Introduce a planner-region bridge table and relate each entity to it with one-to-many relationships.
options.why: Correct. The bridge holds one row per planner-region pair, and both dimensions relate to it one-to-many, resolving the many-to-many cleanly.

options.text: Set the direct relationship to many-to-many cardinality with bidirectional filtering.
options.why: A direct M:N relationship blurs which side filters which and is harder to govern than an explicit bridge.

options.text: Duplicate the planner table once per region.
options.why: Duplication multiplies maintenance and breaks any planner-level attribute or security filtering.

questions.explanation: A bridge (junction) table is the dimensional answer to many-to-many: it materializes the pairs once, and the model reads it through ordinary one-to-many relationships.

questions.title: Cardinality on the bridge
questions.prompt: A bridge table planner_region_bridge has one row per planner-region pair. Which relationship configuration connects it correctly to dim_planner and dim_region?

options.text: One-to-many from dim_planner to the bridge, and one-to-many from dim_region to the bridge.
options.why: Correct. Each dimension is the one-side of its relationship to the bridge, so the bridge carries the resolved many-to-many grain.

options.text: Many-to-one from each dimension to the bridge.
options.why: That points the filters the wrong way; the bridge is the many side of both relationships.

options.text: Many-to-many from dim_planner directly to dim_region, skipping the bridge.
options.why: That abandons the bridge the question establishes and re-creates the ambiguity it was meant to remove.

options.text: One-to-one from each dimension to the bridge.
options.why: One-to-one is wrong: the bridge holds multiple rows per planner and per region.

questions.explanation: The bridge sits at the many end of both relationships: dim_planner 1—* planner_region_bridge *—1 dim_region, with filter direction set deliberately toward the fact side or the dimension side depending on the question being answered.

questions.title: One date table or four
questions.prompt: A model needs order date, ship date, and two snapshot dates. One option marks a single DimDate table and creates inactive relationships for the non-primary dates; another clones the date table per role. Which trade-off statement is accurate?

options.text: Inactive relationships cannot be used by DAX measures at all.
options.why: They can — USERELATIONSHIP activates them inside CALCULATE for the measure's duration.

options.text: A single marked date table with inactive relationships keeps one source of date attributes; measures targeting other roles activate the relationship with USERELATIONSHIP.
options.why: Correct. One marked date table plus USERELATIONSHIP avoids duplicated calendars while still answering role-specific questions.

options.text: Every role-playing date must be a separate physical table or time intelligence breaks.
options.why: Time intelligence works against the marked date table; separate tables are one option, not a requirement.

options.text: Inactive relationships are evaluated on refresh and stored like calculated columns.
options.why: Relationships are query-time structures; nothing about them is materialized at refresh.

questions.explanation: Both designs exist in the wild. The single marked date table with inactive relationships is the lower-maintenance default; USERELATIONSHIP activates a specific role inside a measure.

questions.title: The ambiguous path
questions.prompt: A report author enables bidirectional filtering between DimProduct and FactInventory to make a slicer affect another visual. After the change, some totals differ depending on which visual is evaluated first. What is the soundest review finding?

options.text: Bidirectional filtering is never evaluated, so the totals change must come from refresh timing.
options.why: Bidirectional filtering is evaluated at query time — that is exactly when the order-sensitivity appears.

options.text: The single-direction default should be restored; bidirectional paths create ambiguous filter propagation that can make results context-dependent.
options.why: Correct. Unnecessary bidirectionality is the documented cause of ambiguous, order-sensitive results; the fix is single direction plus deliberate bridge or USERELATIONSHIP design.

options.text: The model needs more bidirectional relationships to make the paths consistent.
options.why: Adding more bidirectionality widens the ambiguity instead of removing it.

options.text: The totals are wrong because bidirectional filtering disables query caching.
options.why: Caching is not the mechanism here; the ambiguity of the filter path is.

questions.explanation: Bidirectional cross-filtering is a targeted tool, not a default. Where it is not required, single-direction propagation keeps one unambiguous filter story.

questions.title: Column or measure
questions.prompt: A developer writes MarginPct = FactSales[Revenue] - FactSales[Cost] as a calculated column, then discovers row-level totals do not match margin computed from aggregated revenue and cost. What explains the discrepancy?

options.text: The column needs to be marked as a measure to aggregate correctly.
options.why: Marking is not the mechanism; the aggregation semantics differ fundamentally.

options.text: A calculated column computes per row and then aggregates the row results, which differs from aggregating revenue and cost separately before subtracting.
options.why: Correct. Row-wise margin then summation equals a different number than (sum revenue − sum cost) whenever margins vary across rows.

options.text: Calculated columns recompute at query time, so the totals raced with the visual.
options.why: Calculated columns materialize at refresh; they do not recompute per query.

options.text: The discrepancy proves RLS is filtering the two visuals differently.
options.why: RLS is irrelevant here; the difference is purely the arithmetic order.

questions.explanation: This is the classic ratio/margin trap: a per-row computed quantity aggregated afterwards is not the same as the same expression evaluated over aggregates. The fix is a measure evaluated in filter context.

questions.title: Generating the calendar
questions.prompt: The model needs a date table spanning 2019-01-01 through today plus the next five years, with year, quarter, month and fiscal columns. The source warehouse has no date dimension. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: A calculated table built with DAX calendar functions, then marked as the model's date table.
options.why: Correct. CALENDAR/CALENDARAUTO in a calculated table plus derived columns, marked as date table, is the documented in-model pattern.

options.text: An implicit date hierarchy from the fact's date column.
options.why: Implicit hierarchies exist but do not produce a proper marked date table; time intelligence against them is unreliable.

options.text: A Power Query parameter that renames the fact's date column.
options.why: Renaming a fact column creates no calendar rows at all.

options.text: Importing the fact table twice and using one copy as the calendar.
options.why: The fact is not a date dimension; its rows follow sales grain, not a continuous calendar.

questions.explanation: When no warehouse date dimension exists, a DAX calculated table (CALENDAR or CALENDARAUTO plus attribute columns), marked as the date table, is the standard remedy.

questions.title: What VAR does not do
questions.prompt: A review comment claims a DAX variable (VAR) can be reassigned later in the same expression to improve performance. Which statement about DAX variables is correct?

options.text: A variable is evaluated once, where it is defined, and its value is constant for the rest of that expression.
options.why: Correct. Variables bind once at their definition point and are immutable afterwards — that single-evaluation property is one of their performance benefits.

options.text: A variable re-evaluates every time its name appears, so naming it once changes nothing.
options.why: That is precisely the misunderstanding: re-references reuse the captured value instead of recomputing.

options.text: A variable can be reassigned by a later VAR with the same name in the same expression.
options.why: Redeclaring the same name in the same scope is an error, not a reassignment.

options.text: A variable stores a pointer to the filter context and re-reads it on use.
options.why: The variable captures a value (including a table) computed at definition; it does not live-link to later context changes.

questions.explanation: DAX variables are evaluated exactly once, at their definition point, in the context that exists there — and they are immutable for the remainder of the expression.

questions.title: The transition inside SUMX
questions.prompt: Total Cost reads: SUMX(FactSales, [Total Cost Measure]). Inside FactSales' row context, [Total Cost Measure] still returns per-filter-context values that respect the current row. What mechanism causes this?

options.text: Measures ignore row context entirely inside iterators.
options.why: They do not: the iterator's row context transforms into an equivalent filter context for the measure invocation.

options.text: Context transition: referencing a measure inside a row context implicitly wraps CALCULATE, converting the row's values into filter context.
options.why: Correct. Measure references trigger an implicit CALCULATE, so each iterated row becomes its own filter context for the measure.

options.text: The measure inherits only the outer filters and forgets the row.
options.why: Forgetting the row would make every iteration identical, which is not what happens.

options.text: SUMX replaces relationships, so the measure reads columns directly.
options.why: Relationships are untouched; the transition is about context, not lineage.

questions.explanation: Context transition is the rule: a measure reference inside row context is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE, promoting the current row's values into filter context.

questions.title: Override or intersect
questions.prompt: A visual filters Region = West. The measure Sales All Regions is defined as CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "West"). Another measure, West Plus Slicer, is defined as CALCULATE([Total Sales], KEEPFILTERS(DimRegion[Region] = "West")). With the slicer on North, what do the two measures return?

options.text: Both return West sales.
options.why: KEEPFILTERS exists precisely because the plain filter argument does not intersect with the slicer.

options.text: Sales All Regions returns West sales; West Plus Slicer returns blank, because KEEPFILTERS intersects the West filter with the existing North filter.
options.why: Correct. Without KEEPFILTERS the filter argument overrides the slicer; with it, the argument must coexist with existing filters — West and North intersect to nothing.

options.text: Both return blank.
options.why: Only the KEEPFILTERS version intersects; the plain version overrides.

options.text: Sales All Regions returns North sales; West Plus Slicer returns West sales.
options.why: That reverses the two behaviors.

questions.explanation: A boolean filter argument in CALCULATE overrides existing filters on the same column unless KEEPFILTERS makes it intersect with them.

questions.title: Clearing the slicer
questions.prompt: A measure should ignore every filter on DimDate but keep all other filters (region, product). Which CALCULATE modification is the clearest, most targeted expression of that intent?

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS(DimDate))
options.why: Correct. REMOVEFILTERS names exactly what it clears and touches nothing else.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(FactSales))
options.why: ALL over the fact table removes filters from the fact's columns — broader than the intent and expressed against the wrong table.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL())
options.why: Bare ALL inside CALCULATE clears filters everywhere, destroying region and product filters too.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(FactSales, FactSales[Date]))
options.why: ALLEXCEPT removes everything except the named columns — the inverse of the requirement, and again on the wrong table.

questions.explanation: REMOVEFILTERS(DimDate) states the intent literally: remove filters from the date table only. ALL-family expressions work but say something broader or inverted.

questions.title: Ship-date revenue
questions.prompt:
Given the model below, which measure returns revenue attributed to the ship date rather than the active order-date relationship?
FactSales[OrderDateKey] -> (active) -> DimDate[DateKey]
FactSales[ShipDateKey] -> (inactive) -> DimDate[DateKey]

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDateKey], DimDate[DateKey]))
options.why: Correct. USERELATIONSHIP activates the specified inactive relationship for this calculation's filter context.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], FactSales[ShipDateKey] = DimDate[DateKey])
options.why: A boolean filter comparing two columns is not valid in that form and does not activate a relationship.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], CROSSFILTER(FactSales[OrderDateKey], DimDate[DateKey], Both))
options.why: CROSSFILTER changes filter direction of the active relationship; it does not switch to the ship-date one.

options.text: CALCULATE([Total Sales], TREATAS(VALUES(DimDate[DateKey]), FactSales[ShipDateKey]))
options.why: TREATAS applies the current date values as a filter on the ship-date column, which approximates but does not use the defined relationship, and fails to propagate other date-table filters correctly.

questions.explanation: USERELATIONSHIP exists exactly for role-playing dates: it names the inactive relationship to activate inside this CALCULATE.
questions.code:
Revenue by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDateKey], DimDate[DateKey])
)

questions.title: SUM or SUMX
questions.prompt: Revenue Per Row needs (Revenue − Discount) evaluated per sales row and then totaled. Which implementation is correct?

options.text: SUM(FactSales[Revenue] - FactSales[Discount])
options.why: SUM takes one column, not an expression; this will not even parse.

options.text: SUMX(FactSales, FactSales[Revenue] - FactSales[Discount])
options.why: Correct. SUMX iterates the table, evaluates the expression per row in row context, and sums the results.

options.text: SUM(FactSales[Revenue]) - SUM(FactSales[Discount]) as a calculated column
options.why: As a calculated column this computes one grand-total difference on every row; as a measure it answers a different question than the row-wise requirement.

options.text: COUNTROWS(FactSales) * AVERAGE(FactSales[Revenue])
options.why: Averaging then multiplying ignores the per-row discount entirely.

questions.explanation: X-suffix iterators (SUMX, MAXX, COUNTX…) exist for per-row expression evaluation: row context per row, aggregation of the results at the end.
questions.code:
Net Revenue =
SUMX(
    FactSales,
    FactSales[Revenue] - FactSales[Discount]
)

questions.title: One definition, every measure
questions.prompt: The team wants Year-to-Date, Quarter-to-Date and Rolling-12 variants of every existing measure without writing three versions of each. Which mechanism provides this at query time?

options.text: A calculation group whose calculation items apply CALCULATE selectors like CALCULATETOP or DATEADD to the selected measure.
options.why: Correct. Calculation items wrap whatever measure is in context (via SELECTEDMEASURE) and are applied at query time — one item set, every measure covered.

options.text: A calculated column that stores the YTD variant of each measure.
options.why: Calculated columns evaluate at refresh against a fixed expression and cannot wrap measures dynamically.

options.text: Field parameters listing the three time variants.
options.why: Field parameters swap which fields a visual shows; they do not transform measure behavior.

options.text: A report-level filter that re-bases totals on the date axis.

questions.title: The twice-computed measure
questions.prompt:
Growth % reads:
DIVIDE([Total Sales] - CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR)), CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR)))
The visual is slow. Which rewrite is the documented performance improvement?

options.text: Capture the prior-year value once in a VAR and reuse it in both the numerator and the denominator.
options.why: Correct. The variable is evaluated once instead of twice, which is exactly the documented reason variables improve DAX performance.

options.text: Replace DIVIDE with the / operator to skip error handling.
options.why: DIVIDE's guard is cheap; removing it saves little and reintroduces divide-by-zero handling problems.

options.text: Wrap the whole expression in CALCULATE to force earlier evaluation.
options.why: A redundant CALCULATE does not deduplicate the DATEADD evaluation.

options.text: Convert the measure to a calculated column so it is precomputed.
options.why: A column freezes the number at refresh and breaks time-intelligence slicing.

questions.explanation: Each DATEADD branch re-evaluates the same prior-year calculation. A variable computes it once — the canonical DAX performance improvement from the labs.
questions.code:
Sales YoY % =
VAR PriorYear =
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR))
RETURN
    DIVIDE([Total Sales] - PriorYear, PriorYear)

questions.title: Splitting the timestamp
questions.prompt: A fact carries a DateTime column with a unique value nearly every second, and the Import model's memory footprint is dominated by it. Which modeling change most reduces memory while preserving both daily and time-of-day analysis?

options.text: Split it into a Date column related to DimDate and a separate low-precision time column (e.g., hour), removing the full-precision timestamp.
options.why: Correct. High-cardinality datetime columns dominate columnar memory; splitting preserves the analyses people actually run while collapsing the distinct-value count.

options.text: Encrypt the timestamp column to improve compression.
options.why: Encryption does not compress; it typically hurts encoding.

options.text: Round the timestamp to seconds — it already is, so no change.
options.why: The column is already second-grained; the cardinality problem remains.

options.text: Move the timestamp into a delimited text column for better dictionary encoding.
options.why: Text encoding of datetimes usually increases size and loses type semantics.

questions.explanation: Cardinality drives VertiPaq memory. The documented pattern for timestamp-heavy facts is date/time separation (and rounding precision to what analysis needs), not encoding tricks.

options.why: It already aggregates the given expression over the YTD window.

questions.explanation: Time intelligence presumes a date dimension: continuous dates, marked as the model's date table, with the measure's expression evaluated over its YTD window.

questions.title: Last year, shifted
questions.prompt: Finance asks for a 'same two weeks, one year earlier' comparison that must also work when the current period shifts by a week. Which function gives the needed flexibility over the fixed one-year shift?

options.text: DATEADD, which shifts the date set by an arbitrary number of intervals (days, months, quarters, years).
options.why: Correct. DATEADD parameterizes both the count and the unit of the shift; SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR is the fixed −1 year special case.

options.text: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, because it accepts an interval argument.
options.why: It accepts none — it is hard-wired to one year back.

options.text: TOTALYTD with a negative year-end.
options.why: TOTALYTD aggregates year-to-date, not a shifted period.

options.text: PARALLELPERIOD, because it always matches arbitrary week offsets.
options.why: PARALLELPERIOD shifts whole periods (month/quarter/year), not week-grained windows.

questions.explanation: DATEADD is the general shifter; SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR is literally documented as DATEADD(dates, -1, year). When the offset must vary, DATEADD is the tool.

questions.title: One value or many
questions.prompt: A card visual shows the selected store's name, but errors out when a user selects several stores. Which pattern returns the single store name when exactly one is selected and a friendly fallback otherwise?

options.text: SELECTEDVALUE(DimStore[StoreName], "Multiple stores selected")
options.why: Correct. SELECTEDVALUE returns the value only when exactly one is in context, else the alternate result.

options.text: MAX(DimStore[StoreName])
options.why: MAX returns the alphabetically-last name of many — a plausible-looking wrong answer.

options.text: HASONEVALUE(DimStore[StoreName])
options.why: HASONEVALUE returns TRUE/FALSE; on its own it does not produce the name.

options.text: VALUES(DimStore[StoreName])
options.why: VALUES returns the table of selected names; a card cannot render a multi-row table.

questions.explanation: SELECTEDVALUE is the information-function idiom for 'the one selected value or a fallback'; HASONEVALUE/ISFILTERED are its building blocks for conditional logic.

questions.title: Previous row, ranked
questions.prompt: The team needs a measure returning the previous month's revenue within each region, ordered by date — without relying on time intelligence. Which modern DAX mechanism fits?

options.text: The window functions (OFFSET/INDEX/WINDOW) with ORDERBY on the date and PARTITIONBY on region.
options.why: Correct. DAX window functions compute relative rows over an ordered, partitioned set — the documented mechanism for previous/next/ranked lookups.

options.text: CALCULATE with a REMOVEFILTERS over the whole date table.
options.why: Clearing filters does not address the 'previous row in an ordering' requirement.

options.text: A calculated column storing LAG() over the fact.
options.why: LAG is T-SQL window syntax, not DAX.

options.text: EARLIER inside a calculated column.
options.why: EARLIER navigates nested row contexts at refresh time; it is not a query-time windowing tool.

questions.explanation: OFFSET, INDEX and WINDOW bring SQL-style windowing to DAX: ORDERBY defines the sequence, PARTITIONBY the group, and the function addresses a relative or absolute row.
questions.code:
Prev Month Revenue =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    OFFSET(-1, ALLSELECTED(DimDate[Month]), ORDERBY(DimDate[Month], ASC))
)

questions.title: Static or dynamic
questions.prompt: Each planner may cover two regions. A role filter is needed so planners see only their regions. Which implementation scales without creating one role per planner?

options.text: A dynamic role filtering DimPlanner with USERPRINCIPALNAME() joined through the planner-region bridge.
options.why: Correct. One role, one DAX filter on the signed-in user's principal name, resolved through the mapping table — the documented dynamic RLS pattern.

options.text: Three hundred static roles, one per planner, each with a literal region filter.
options.why: Static roles work but do not scale to hundreds of members or changing assignments.

options.text: A visual-level filter comparing the planner's email to a slicer.
options.why: Visual filters are not security: they hide rows in one visual while the data stays queryable elsewhere.

options.text: Removing the region column from the model entirely.
options.why: That removes the analysis dimension instead of securing it.

questions.explanation: Dynamic RLS maps the signed-in principal (USERPRINCIPALNAME) to permitted rows through a mapping table — one role instead of one per member.

questions.title: Who may read the Delta
questions.prompt: harborline_sales is Direct Lake over the lakehouse. A planner with model access reports being able to see model metadata but failing to read certain tables' data. What does the Direct Lake security model say is in play?

options.text: Direct Lake reads respect OneLake data access roles on the underlying tables in addition to the semantic model's own permissions and RLS.
options.why: Correct. Direct Lake binds to OneLake data, so data-access permissions on that path participate alongside model roles and row-level security.

options.text: Semantic model RLS alone always overrides storage permissions for Direct Lake models.
options.why: Model RLS filters rows; it does not grant read on storage the principal cannot access.

options.text: The planner needs the workspace admin role to query Direct Lake models.
options.why: Admin is neither necessary nor sufficient for data-path access; least privilege applies.

options.text: Direct Lake ignores all permission layers and relies on Entra group membership alone.
options.why: Multiple layers compose; membership alone is not the whole story.

questions.explanation: Direct Lake's data path reaches OneLake storage, so the documented security picture composes model permissions, RLS, and OneLake data access roles — a failure on any layer surfaces as exactly this symptom.

caseStudy.title: Harborline Retail semantic model redesign
caseStudy.text: Harborline Retail runs a Fabric lakehouse (harborline_lake) with Delta tables for roughly two billion point-of-sale rows (fact_sales), product, store, and customer dimensions, and a small daily stock-snapshot fact (fact_stock). The team publishes a Direct Lake semantic model, harborline_sales, on the lakehouse for about 300 store planners. Planners belong to region assignments stored in a planner-region mapping table, and one planner may cover two regions. Finance keeps a separate nightly Import model for regulated reporting. The analytics engineering team ships both models through deployment pipelines and tracks query speed, model size and access reviews monthly. Current friction: a handful of visuals run noticeably slower than the rest, month-start loads overlap with planner working hours, and product hierarchy changes do not appear until someone updates the model.

questions.title: OLS hides the object
questions.prompt: A compensation column must be invisible to planners — not just its values, but its very existence in field lists. Which mechanism provides this, and what is a documented constraint when combining it with RLS?

options.text: Object-level security secures tables/columns (hiding them from metadata); OLS and RLS cannot be defined on the same table.
options.why: Correct. OLS hides objects themselves, and the documented limitation is that a table carries OLS or RLS, not both.

options.text: Dynamic data masking replaces values with *** in the model.
options.why: Masking obscures values but leaves the object visible, and masking is a warehouse feature, not a semantic-model OLS substitute.

options.text: Renaming the column to a non-obvious name in the model.
options.why: Obscurity is not security; the field is still exposed.

options.text: Removing the column from report visuals only.
options.why: Visual edits are cosmetic; the column remains queryable.

questions.explanation: Object-level security removes the object from the metadata the principal can see — and the documented combination rule is OLS or RLS per table, not both.

questions.title: Deploy over XMLA
questions.prompt: The team wants to manage harborline_sales from tabular tooling (SSMS, Tabular Editor) including writes: deploy model changes and process partitions. What must be true about the workspace's XMLA endpoint setting, and what capability follows?

options.text: The XMLA endpoint must be set to read-write, which enables metadata deployment and partition processing with tools like SSMS and Tabular Editor.
options.why: Correct. Read-write is the documented setting for XMLA write scenarios — deployment and processing — while read-only supports analysis tools only.

options.text: Read-only suffices; deployments ride the same channel as refreshes.
options.why: Read-only is exactly that: reads. Writes require the read-write setting.

options.text: XMLA writes happen through the deployment pipeline UI instead of the endpoint.
options.why: Pipelines are a separate feature; XMLA write is the endpoint's own capability.

options.text: XMLA endpoint settings apply only to Import models, never Direct Lake.
options.why: The endpoint governs the workspace's models, including Direct Lake, subject to the documented capability matrix.

questions.explanation: The study guide's 'Deploy and manage semantic models by using the XMLA endpoint' maps to the read-write endpoint setting, which unlocks tabular tooling for deployment and processing.
